extracted.intended_audience: legislators, administrators, trade policymakers, trade lawyers and legal scholars interested in Canadian anti-dumping procedure and tribunal practice
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of the legal, procedural and administrative standards governing anti-dumping investigations and the Anti-dumping Tribunal in Canada, including statutory definitions, investigative thresholds, tribunal powers, confidentiality, remedies, and procedural timeframes. Intended to guide evaluation of tribunal procedure and possible reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of dumping
rubrics_metrics.description: Dumping is the sale for export at prices lower than those charged to domestic buyers ('normal value'), taking into account the conditions and terms of sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as international price discrimination enabled by separate markets and some degree of monopoly power; may be intentional (to secure foreign exchange, protect home market, meet foreign competition, or for predatory purposes) or occasionally unintentional. The margin of dumping is the difference between normal value and export price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of countervailing duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A special duty levied to offset a direct or indirect subsidy of manufacture, production or export.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Article VI paragraph 3, countervailing duty may not exceed the bounty or subsidy bestowed; treated separately from dumping duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export price (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The export price is, in general, the lesser of the exporter's sale price and the importer's purchase price (subsection 10(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is no reliable sale/purchase price (e.g., associated persons, compensatory arrangements), the statute permits deeming the export price by formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal value (definition and computation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to subsection (5), the normal value of goods is the price of like goods when sold by the exporter (a) to purchasers with whom the exporter is not associated, (b) in the ordinary course of trade for home consumption under competitive conditions, (c) during a prescribed period related to the time of the sale to the importer, and (d) at the place from which the goods were shipped (section 9(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjustments must be made for differences in terms/conditions of sale, taxation and other price comparability factors as prescribed by regulation. Subsection 9(5)(a) permits DM, in certain circumstances, to determine normal value by aggregating cost of production plus allowances for administrative, selling and other costs and profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margin of dumping
rubrics_metrics.description: The margin of dumping of any goods is the amount by which the normal value of the goods exceeds the export price (section 8(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-dumping duties imposed shall not exceed the margin of dumping (Article VI paragraph 2). Provisional duties also must not be greater than the margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article VI requirement: material injury or retardation
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-dumping action is permitted only if dumping 'causes or threatens material injury to an established industry... or materially retards the establishment of a domestic industry' (Article VI paragraph 1 and 6(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dumping alone is not sufficient; a demonstrated effect of material injury or threat/retardation is required before duties can be imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-dumping Code: like product (Article 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'like product' is defined as a product identical in all respects to the product under consideration or, failing that, another product with characteristics closely resembling those of the product under consideration (Article 2(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application raises practical difficulties (e.g., components, product differentiation) discussed in Chapter IV; selection of comparable sales must account for levels of trade and comparable quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation standard (Article 3: 'principal cause')
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (a) permits a determination of injury only when dumping is 'demonstrably the principal cause' of material injury, threat, or retardation; authorities must weigh the effect of dumping against 'all other factors taken together' (Article 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase 'principal cause' has caused difficulty; in practice it is generally considered sufficient that dumping be a cause (and material), perhaps more significant than any other single cause, so long as other factors are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'domestic industry' and 'major proportion' (Article 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'domestic industry' refers to domestic producers as a whole of the like products or to those whose collective output constitutes a major proportion of total domestic production (Article 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geneva discussions suggested 'major proportion' means a substantial proportion, in practice more than half, but Canadian authorities (Ministry, Tribunal, Federal Court) have applied differing interpretations; Article 4(a)(ii) allows separate industry status in geographically segmented markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous consideration of dumping and injury (Article 5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigating authorities are required to consider evidence of both dumping and injury simultaneously (Article 5(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study notes that Canada may be in breach of this obligation and discusses implications for procedure and fairness in Chapter VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential information protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 6(b)-(d) of the Code and subsection 29(3) of the Act require protection of confidential business information provided during inquiries; confidential evidence/information 'shall not be made public in such a manner as to be available for the use of any business competitor or rival' (29(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulties arise in practice over access to and handling of confidential material; confidentiality affects transparency, party participation, and tribunal fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price undertakings as alternative remedy (Article 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-dumping proceedings may be terminated without imposition of duties if exporters give voluntary undertakings to revise prices to eliminate the margin of dumping or to cease exporting at dumped prices (Article 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study suggests price undertakings may sometimes be a more satisfactory and less formal solution than duties, and discusses their practical use in Chapter VIII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional measures and provisional duty limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional duty may be imposed during the period between the preliminary determination and the Tribunal finding, but duty must not be greater than the margin of dumping (defined by the Act and the Code). Section 15 requires provisional duty or posting security not greater than the margin where a preliminary determination has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 10 provides for provisional measures; the provisional period and refund/adjustment rules apply when final findings differ from preliminary calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deputy Minister initiation and preliminary determination thresholds (sections 13 and 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deputy Minister (DM) must initiate an investigation if he is of the opinion there is evidence of dumping and either he believes or the Tribunal advises there is evidence that dumping has caused/is likely to cause material injury or retardation (13(1)). If satisfied dumping exists with non-negligible margin and volume, subsection 14(1) requires him to make a 'preliminary determination' of dumping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If DM finds insufficient evidence of dumping, negligible margin/volume, or no evidence of material injury, he shall terminate the investigation (13(6)). DM or complainant may refer injury questions to the Tribunal (13(3), 13(7)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligible margin/volume as termination ground
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigation shall be terminated without a preliminary determination when the DM finds insufficient evidence of dumping, a negligible margin of dumping or volume of dumped goods, or no evidence of material injury or retardation (13(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute treats 'negligible' margin/volume as a threshold below which proceedings are not pursued; practical interpretation of 'negligible' affects whether provisional measures and hearings occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal inquiry responsibilities and scope (section 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of a notice of a preliminary determination, the Tribunal shall inquire whether dumping has caused/is causing/is likely to cause material injury or has materially retarded establishment of production (16(1)(a)). Paragraph 16(1)(f) requires inquiry into whether considerable importation has occurred causing material injury, whether the importer was or should have been aware of injurious dumping, and whether duty should be assessed to prevent recurrence. The Tribunal has 90 days to make an order or finding (16(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal may direct the DM to investigate related dumping (16(2)); it must produce a finding within statutory time; its inquiries are focused on causal relationship, injury, import volumes, and importer knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal judicial powers and 'court of record' status (section 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal is a 'court of record' and, as regards attendance, swearing and examination of witnesses, production and inspection of documents, enforcement of orders, inspection of property and other matters, has all powers, rights and privileges vested in a superior court of record (27(1)-(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This designation has led to increased formality in Tribunal procedures and has been a basis for judicial criticism; the exact consequences of 'court of record' status are unclear and debated in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing and procedural formality (sections 25, 29)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal may make procedural rules (25). Parties may appear in person, by counsel or agent; hearings may be held in camera or in public at Tribunal or Chairman's discretion (29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 29(3) imposes confidentiality limits on publication of confidential business information elicited during inquiry. The study assesses whether formality and in-camera practice are desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal membership, appointment and chair powers (section 21, 23)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal consists of not more than five members appointed by Governor in Council, holding office during good behaviour for seven years; a Chairman and Vice-Chairman are designated (21). The Chairman is chief executive and assigns members to hearings (23(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational features (background of personnel, finances, assignment of work) influence Tribunal functioning and are discussed in Chapter V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review, rescind, change or re-hear authority (section 31)
rubrics_metrics.description: After any order or finding, the Tribunal may review, rescind, change or alter the order or finding, or re-hear any matter before deciding it (section 31).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original privative clause preventing judicial review was removed by the Federal Court Act; the Tribunal retains internal mechanisms to revisit its decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final determination, assessment of duty and appeals (sections 17-20)
rubrics_metrics.description: After receipt of Tribunal order/finding, the Deputy Minister must make a final determination and assess the duty payable or return provisional duty/security (17). Appeals from the DM's final determination/redetermination and reappraisal lie to the Tariff Board, and then on questions of law to the Federal Court of Canada (sections 19-20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 18-20 set out appraisal, reappraisal, and appellate pathways; provisional duties collected may be refunded if final findings do not support them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory rules for price comparability and adjustments (Regulations 3-19A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations prescribe selection of sales at appropriate trade level and comparable quantities (Reg.3); adjustment of normal value for quantity discounts (4), quality/structure/design/material differences (5), deferred or cash discounts (6-7), transport costs (8); further rules cover trade level adjustments, rebates of internal taxes, duty drawbacks, exchange rates, computation periods, transit through third countries, costs of export and compensatory arrangements (Regs.9-19A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory detail determines how normal value and export price are computed in practice, including trade-level comparability and allowance calculations; many practical computational difficulties arise under these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 11 deeming and constructive valuation when information lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11 permits the Deputy Minister to prescribe a means of determining the normal value or export price when sufficient information has not been furnished or is not available to apply sections 9 or 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically important: when exporters do not provide reliable data, DM can use formulae or construct values (including aggregating cost-plus allowances), with significant effects on margin calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of components and like goods in margin computation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Code and Act address dumping of components and the difficulty of establishing 'like goods' when goods contain imported components (Article 2(e) and discussion in Chapter IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical issues arise in allocating costs, comparing levels of trade, and deciding whether components constitute the same like product as finished goods; Canadian application has produced controversy and requires careful factual analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative and procedural flow (complaint, DM initiation, Tribunal referral, preliminary sitting, provisional entry, finding, final determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical procedural sequence: complaint received or DM may initiate; initial enquiries; DM may terminate or initiate investigation; where preliminary determination of dumping is made, provisional duty or security is applied and goods may be entered provisionally; DM refers to Tribunal; Tribunal holds preliminary sitting/hearing and makes a finding; provisional period ends; if injury finding, DM makes final determination and duties assessed; if no injury finding, proceedings terminated and provisional duties refunded (Appendix D flow chart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either DM or complainant may refer injury questions to Tribunal at multiple stages; the flowchart summarizes statutory triggers, decision points, refund and termination consequences, and terms such as 'considerable importation' and 'negligible' used at decision gates.
